Two hundred of them boiling up off the face of the wax all at once, each about as long as the fae's own hand, every one the same small round furred amber-and-umber shape, the whole mass rising in one heaving dome — one riding the smoke upward like a lift, legs dangling.

A broad circling ring of sixty or more going round and round like weather, each no longer than two of the little wax cups across, all the same clean shape, the ring tilting as she tilts, one passenger sitting quietly on top of her rolled grass-cord line.

A hundred of them streaming in one long curving current from somewhere off to the left, each about as long as the fae's own hand, every one the same furred shape at speed, the whole current banking hard and going straight for the broken wax edge.

The mass parted into two equal currents either side of the drifting smoke and rejoining beyond it, a hundred in each arm, every one no longer than two of the little wax cups across, the whole thing moving like river water parting round a stone.

Four hundred of them hanging in a column off the lower hem of the wax sheet, each about as long as the fae's own hand, all the same size, the column swaying slowly left — one at the very base going in a small determined circle.

A carpet of them packed so tight across one wax sheet the wax only shows in thin gaps, two hundred at least, every one no longer than two of the little wax cups across, each the same furred shape, three more sitting in a row watching from a taut grass cord.

Sixty or more arriving back all at once from off to the right, each about as long as the fae's own hand, every one the same compact amber shape, landing in a single wave that covers half the wax face, one of them landing directly on the fae's outstretched wrist and staying.

The whole air full of them, four hundred strong, each no longer than two of the little wax cups across, every one the same small round furred shape, the light between them coming through in scattered grains, the mass turning as one slow wheel.

A hundred of them all facing outward on the wax with their wings shivering in unison, each about as long as the fae's own hand, every one the same shape and size, making the whole sheet tremble as if it breathed — one facing the wrong way entirely.

Forty or more dropping straight down off the wax edge in a loose curtain, each no longer than two of the little wax cups across, every one the same furred amber-and-umber shape, the curtain billowing once before they pull themselves level and turn outward.

A hundred of them massing on the underside of the lowest sheet, each about as long as the fae's own hand, every one the same small dense shape clinging upside down, the whole ceiling of them shivering — one hanging by a single leg, the rest of its body swinging free.

Two hundred streaming back in a long loaded line from somewhere off the left, each no longer than two of the little wax cups across, every one the same clean shape, the line so orderly it looks braided, one in the middle flying sideways for reasons of its own.

The mass gone quiet and low and clung flat to the wax, three hundred of them and every one the same small furred shape, only a dozen out in the air and each of those about as long as the fae's own hand, hovering in a loose slow ring.

A hundred of them boiling up where a slab of wax has just come free, each about as long as the fae's own hand, every one the same round shape, the cloud blooming upward and outward as if the wax itself exhaled — one going straight up and not stopping.

Forty or more riding the underside of the smoke column, each no longer than two of the little wax cups across, all the same furred shape, moving against the smoke's own drift, the whole cluster inching steadily upward together, one going round the smoke rather than through it.

A broad slow spiral of two hundred descending toward the wax, each about as long as the fae's own hand, every one the same small amber shape, the spiral tightening as it nears the surface, one at the outermost edge going the wrong direction round.

Three hundred of them covering every face of the hanging wax in a single dense layer, each no longer than two of the little wax cups across, every one the same furred shape and size, the whole surface alive and shifting — one walking in a straight line across all the others.

Sixty or more streaming up the far side of the wax sheet and pouring over its top edge in a wave, each about as long as the fae's own hand, all the same compact shape, the wave cresting and spreading down the near face in a rush.

A hundred of them hanging motionless in the air in a broad flat disc, each no longer than two of the little wax cups across, every one the same round furred shape, all facing the same direction — one sitting on the disc's exact centre as if it had called the meeting.

Two hundred boiling off the wax all together in a single pulse, each about as long as the fae's own hand, every one the same shape, the pulse going outward evenly in all directions — one breaking off early and heading the other way with apparent purpose.

Forty or more packed shoulder to shoulder along a grass-cord line strung between two twig-pegs, each no longer than two of the little wax cups across, every one the same furred amber shape, all facing along the cord, one at the far end facing back toward the others.

The whole mass splitting suddenly into two clouds of a hundred each, every one about as long as the fae's own hand and the same small round shape, each cloud sweeping away in a different arc and coming back together ten body-lengths off to the right.

A hundred of them walking in long slow circles on the open wax face, each no longer than two of the little wax cups across, every one the same shape, the circles overlapping and interlocking — one walking a very small tight circle directly in the centre, not joining the larger pattern.

Four hundred of them streaming off the back of the wax sheet and round its lower edge in a continuous river, each about as long as the fae's own hand, every one the same furred amber-and-umber shape, the river never thinning — one riding the current backward, facing upstream.

Sixty or more hanging in a loose swaying cloud just off the wax face, each no longer than two of the little wax cups across, all the same compact shape, the whole cloud breathing slowly in and out, one at the very surface hovering in place and not touching the mass.
